content: Aspartic acid, also known as Asp or D, is an α-amino acid with the chemical formula HO₂CCH(NH₂)CH₂CO₂H. The carboxylate anion form of aspartic acid is referred to as aspartate. Aspartic acid is one of the building blocks of proteins, and its codons are GAU and GAC. Aspartate plays a significant role in biosynthesis. Like all amino acids, the presence of acidic protons in aspartic acid depends on the local chemical environment of the residue and the pH of the solution. Aspartic acid was first discovered in 1827 by Plisson, who synthesized it by boiling asparagine (discovered in 1806) with a base. The term aspartic acid can refer to either of two stereoisomers or a mixture of both. Of these, only the L-isomer, L-aspartic acid, is directly incorporated into proteins. The D-isomer, D-aspartic acid, has more limited biological roles. Enzymatic synthesis typically produces one specific isomer, while chemical synthesis often yields a racemic mixture of both forms, known as DL-aspartic acid. In mammals, aspartate is a non-essential amino acid, as it can be synthesized from oxaloacetate via transamination. In plants and microorganisms, aspartate serves as a precursor for the biosynthesis of several amino acids, including four essential ones: methionine, threonine, isoleucine, and lysine. The conversion of aspartate into these amino acids begins with the reduction of aspartate to its semialdehyde form, O₂CCH(NH₂)CH₂CHO. Additionally, asparagine is derived from aspartate through a transamidation reaction involving glutamine and glutamic acid. Aspartate also has other biochemical roles. It is a metabolite in the urea cycle and participates in gluconeogenesis. It carries reducing equivalents in the malate-aspartate shuttle, which involves the interconversion of aspartate and oxaloacetate, the oxidized derivative of malic acid. Furthermore, aspartate donates a nitrogen atom during the biosynthesis of inosine, a precursor to purine bases. Aspartate, the conjugate base of aspartic acid, acts as a neurotransmitter. It stimulates NMDA receptors, although less potently than glutamate, another amino acid neurotransmitter. Aspartate functions as an excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain and is classified as an excitotoxin. Aspartic acid is not an essential amino acid for humans, meaning it can be synthesized from intermediates of central metabolic pathways. It is found in various dietary sources, including: Animal sources: luncheon meats, sausage meat, and wild game. Vegetable sources: sprouting seeds, oat flakes, avocado, asparagus, young sugarcane, and molasses derived from sugar beets. Dietary supplements: available as aspartic acid itself or as salts, such as magnesium aspartate. Artificial sweeteners: aspartame (marketed under brands like NutraSweet, Equal, and Canderel). Racemic aspartic acid can also be synthesized chemically from diethyl sodium phthalimidomalonate, a compound with the formula C₆H₄(CO)₂NC(CO₂Et)₂.
